sections.h2: What should you know before selling a house in Westerville, Ohio?
sections.html:
Westerville is a northeast suburb of Columbus that straddles two counties, Franklin and Delaware, and that split decides which auditor, which board of revision and which health district you deal with. The Census Bureau lists 12.60 square miles of land and estimates 38,165 residents on July 1, 2025, down from 39,190 in the 2020 census.

Westerville runs its own electric and water utilities and does not collect property tax at all. The sections below start with where your parcel sits and then walk through the city steps, county filings and state paperwork for a sale.

sections.h2: How did Westerville become the Dry Capital of the World?
sections.html:
Settlers arrived around 1810, and the town took its name from the Westervelt family, who moved from New York in 1818. Otterbein University traces to a seminary chartered in 1839 and was renamed in 1847. The town was platted by 1856 and incorporated in August 1858.

An 1859 ordinance banned alcohol sales, and in 1909 the Anti-Saloon League moved its national headquarters to Westerville. The town stayed dry for most of the 20th century and was known as the Dry Capital of the World. In 1916 Westerville became the first village in Ohio to adopt a council-manager form of government, which it keeps today. A 1995 annexation of 941 acres to the north brought in alcohol-selling businesses, and voters later approved alcohol sales at specific locations in the old town.

The old town sits around Uptown Westerville and Otterbein, and the 1995 annexation added land to the north.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about owning in Westerville?
sections.html:
Census QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 describe a mid-priced suburb with a settled owner base.

  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 72.5%.
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $374,500.
  • Median monthly owner costs: $2,120 with a mortgage and $968 without one.
  • Median gross rent: $1,364.
  • Households: 15,208, at 2.43 people per household.
  • Median household income: $109,404; 57.9% of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher.
  • Residents 65 and older: 21.5%.

Mean travel time to work is 19.4 minutes. Interstates 71 and 270 border the city, State Route 3 runs through Uptown as State Street, and central Westerville is about 16 miles from downtown Columbus and 12 miles from John Glenn Columbus International Airport by interstate.

sections.h2: Which county handles your Westerville house?
sections.html:
The city sits across the Franklin and Delaware county line, so start with the auditor's parcel search to see which county bills your house. The city itself collects no property tax. Franklin County Auditor's office is at 614-525-4663 and Delaware County Auditor's office is at 740-833-2900.

Delaware's board says it reviews value as of the January 1 lien date and does not hear complaints about taxes. Hearings usually take 10 to 20 minutes, and an appeal goes to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or the county Court of Common Pleas within 30 days of the decision letter.

sections.h2: What does the Westerville Building Division require?
sections.html:
The Building Division is a state-certified department inside Planning and Development, reachable at 614-901-6650. It reviews plans before work starts and issues a Certificate of Occupancy or a Final Approval after inspections. Permit fees are paid when you pick up the permit, and plans go in through the city's Plan Review Portal.

  • Permits cover new buildings, alterations, signs, fences, pools, patio covers, decks, garages and satellite dishes, and fences carry no permit fee.
  • The city does not require a homeowner or contractor to hold a city license before pulling a permit.
  • A home occupation can need a conditional use permit.
  • Since 2021 the division reports nearly 700 residential permits with about $40.7 million in construction value.

Ask the division for your permit history before you list, and close out any permit that never received a final approval.

sections.h2: How do utilities and trash work when a Westerville house changes hands?
sections.html:
Westerville supplies electric and water service itself, while sewer treatment comes through Columbus and refuse through Rumpke. All four charges appear on one bill that is due on the 15th of the month after it is issued. Utility Billing sits at 21 S. State Street and answers at 614-901-6430. Sewer charges follow water use.

  • Refuse and recycling go out every Tuesday, and yard waste goes out every Monday.
  • Large items such as stoves and furniture can go to the curb on collection day, but air conditioners and refrigerators must go through outside vendors.
  • The city requires owners to keep yards and vacant lots free of trash, debris, overgrown grass and weeds. Code Enforcement takes calls at 614-901-6650.
  • A garage sale needs no permit, but it is limited to one every six months and three consecutive days.

Schedule the final meter reading with Utility Billing as part of the closing checklist so the buyer's service starts clean.

sections.h2: What do snow and storm rules mean for a Westerville seller?
sections.html:
Winter showings run into city rules. Plows clear all city streets once snow passes two inches, and a snow emergency starts automatically above three inches, after which cars left on the street can be towed. Owners must keep the walkway in front of the house clear of snow and ice.

Storms bring a second set of rules. The city removes fallen limbs from street trees, but a tree or branch that comes down from private property is the owner's job to remove. Westerville also offers free residential fire inspections at 614-901-6600, which gives a seller a quick safety check before a buyer's inspector arrives.

sections.h2: Which schools and employers draw buyers to Westerville?
sections.html:
The Westerville City School District has three high schools: South, which is an International Baccalaureate school, North and Central. Its middle schools are Blendon, Genoa, Heritage, Minerva Park and Walnut Springs.

The city's 2023 financial report lists JPMorgan Chase as the top employer at 3,471 workers, followed by Mount Carmel Health System at 3,293, Westerville City Schools at 1,836 and Otterbein University at 1,533. The Central Ohio Transit Authority runs five bus lines through the city, though Westerville operates no buses of its own.

sections.h2: What must an Ohio seller deliver in Westerville?
sections.html:
Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 applies to sales of homes with one to four units. The seller completes the state disclosure form and delivers a signed copy to the buyer or the buyer's agent. Receiving it late opens a short rescission window, so hand it over before the offer is signed.

Value disputes follow ORC 5715.19: the complaint is due by March 31 of the next year, or the first-half collection closing date if that falls later. The tax year 2025 window closed March 31, 2026 in both counties.

faqs.q: Does the City of Westerville collect property taxes?
faqs.a: No. The city's service page says county governments collect property taxes for every taxing district. Call the Franklin County Auditor at 614-525-4663 or the Delaware County Auditor at 740-833-2900, depending on where your parcel sits.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to build a fence before I sell a Westerville house?
faqs.a: Yes, a permit is required to build, replace, relocate or alter a fence, though the city charges no permit fee. Call the Zoning Division at 614-901-6662.

faqs.q: Who collects trash at a Westerville house?
faqs.a: Refuse and recycling are collected Tuesdays and yard waste Mondays, and Rumpke provides refuse service. Containers go out no earlier than 6 p.m. the evening before and no later than 7 a.m. on collection day.

faqs.q: What is Westerville's income tax rate?
faqs.a: The city's service page lists 2.00%, and all adult residents and businesses file city returns. Ask the city's tax office at 614-901-6420 how a sale affects your filing.

faqs.q: How do I find out which county my Westerville house is in?
faqs.a: Search the parcel on either county auditor's website, or look at the property tax bill. Franklin and Delaware counties run separate boards of revision, health districts and auditor offices.
